title: look at something bigger than you today
hook: look at something bigger than you today
tomorrow: every tradition says it: you can't do this alone

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: enough. Your line was the same word: enough. When the wanting started up, did you look at what was already in your hands? Day nineteen.

The ocean, seen for the first time. A storm rolling in over a field. A night sky far from any city, so full of stars it looks fake. A newborn's hand. Moments like these can stop a person in their tracks. For a second, the self goes quiet. The problems don't vanish, they just get smaller, because something else got very big. And it's easy to go weeks without one, eyes down: on screens, on sidewalks, on lists. So today comes with an assignment. Look at something bigger than you. Today's word is awe.

segments.voice: In 1836, the American writer Ralph Waldo Emerson published a little book called Nature. Early in it he asks you to imagine something: "If the stars should appear one night in a thousand years, how would men believe and adore". His point is that they do appear, every clear night. The wonder is always on offer, to anyone who looks up. The Psalms looked at the same night sky, long before: "When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; What is man, that thou art mindful of him?" Notice the move. Look at the vast thing, and the question comes back to you: how small I am, and how strange that I'm here at all. Now the lab. Researchers who study awe, including the psychologist Dacher Keltner at Berkeley, find it has a signature: people describe feeling small, and it isn't a bad feeling. The self shrinks, and the world opens. In one study, people spent one minute looking up at a grove of very tall eucalyptus trees, while others looked at a tall building. Then a researcher stumbled and dropped a handful of pens. The people who'd been looking up at the trees picked up more of them. One minute of awe, and people were a little more helpful. Some astronauts who've seen the whole earth from space describe a version of this too, sometimes called the overview effect. An essayist, a psalmist, a lab: they hold very different beliefs about what's behind the stars. The move they describe is the same. Look up, and come back down a little different.
screen: `ONE NIGHT IN A THOUSAND YEARS.` · `WHEN I CONSIDER THY HEAVENS.` · `SMALL, AND IT ISN'T BAD.` · `THE TREES AND THE DROPPED PENS.` · then, large: `LOOK UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If you can, look out a window, or step outside. Find the biggest thing you can see: the sky, a tree, a building, the clouds. If you're stuck inside, close your eyes and remember the biggest thing you've ever stood under. For the next seventy-five seconds, just look. Let it be big. Let yourself be small next to it. You don't need to name what you feel. The bell holds the time.
Awe. The feeling of standing next to something vast, and getting a little smaller, and a little more generous. Nineteenth word.
Your line: look up. Once today, on purpose, stop and look up: at the sky, the trees, the ceiling of an old building. Give it thirty seconds. Day nineteen.

screen: `DAY 19 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EVERY TRADITION SAYS IT: YOU CAN'T DO THIS ALONE.`

howItsDone: Some people seek awe on purpose: through walks in nature, stargazing, pilgrimages to mountains and great buildings, or by pausing, as the Psalms do, to consider the night sky.
